title: The Largely Equine History of Veterinary Medicine
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of veterinary medicine, from early evidence of animal healing in ancient Mesopotamia (Lagash) through medieval farriers and cow leeches, Gervase Markham's horse care book, Claude Bourgelat's veterinary schools in France, the rinderpest and horse plagues, the founding of the US Veterinary Medical Association in 1863, the automobile's impact on horse-focused practices, the shift to dogs and cats led by Maria Dickin's PDSA and Louis Moody, and Lila Miller's shelter medicine reforms. The episode closes with a listener mail segment from Ian Bowers listing favorite tangents.
topics: PDSA People's Dispensary for Sick Animals

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the word 'livestock' and 'mast' and introduce the topic of veterinary history, noting the research came from an article by Olivia.

segments.title: Ancient origins and early animal care
segments.summary: Earliest unambiguous evidence of medical care for animals is in Lagash around 4100 years ago, with an expert healer named La Ladina mentioned. Care likely predates this with animal domestication. Early care focused on diet and herbs, and the word veterinarian derives from a Latin verb meaning to draw.

segments.title: Medieval farriers and cow leeches
segments.summary: In medieval Europe, animal care was largely for status animals. In Britain and the US, farriers who shod horses also trimmed hooves and performed some surgeries such as cutting horses, and cow leeches treated sick cattle. Knowledge was passed on through apprenticeship with no book learning.

segments.title: Gervase Markham's horse care book
segments.summary: Gervase Markham's 1600s book Markham's Masterpiece was a go-to horse care text for over 200 years. It included useful advice but also bad practices such as leech bloodletting and purging, alongside herbal remedies.

segments.title: Claude Bourgelat and the first veterinary schools
segments.summary: Claude Bourgelat, a riding academy instructor, wrote a book in 1750 and persuaded King Louis XV to fund a horse veterinary school, which was first set up in Lyon. The schools spread to Vienna in 1767, then to London, Berlin and elsewhere. Rinderpest, which killed about 200 million cattle in Europe, turned the temporary grant into permanent state support.

segments.title: American horse care and horse plague of the 1870s
segments.summary: American farmers were expected to care for their own animals with little formal veterinary training. A horse epidemic in the 1870s left horses sick, and during the Great Boston Fire of 1872 firefighters had to respond on foot. The ASPCA was given policing powers in New York City to inspect sick horses. Rural healers still used charms, such as a Pennsylvania healer's spell for bots.

segments.title: Professionalization and the US Veterinary Medical Association
segments.summary: In 1863 veterinary surgeons from seven states met in New York City and founded the U.S. Veterinary Medical Association, now the American Veterinary Medical Association. Josiah H. Stickney, a Harvard Medical School graduate, was its first president. Congress required cavalry regiments to have a farrier with a veterinary college degree. Many for-profit veterinary schools followed with uneven quality, mostly in cities. The automobile then displaced horses and many schools closed by the late 1920s.

segments.title: Shift to dogs: Maria Dickin and Louis Moody
segments.summary: With horses declining, veterinarians began treating dogs, which they had previously avoided. Maria Dickin founded the People's Dispensary for Sick Animals (PDSA) in Britain, offering free treatment for the poor. Veterinary surgeons later worked with it, and the Royal College of Veterinary Surgeons pushed for involvement after a large bequest. New York veterinarian Louis Moody dedicated his life to cats after a cat saved him in a house fire and wrote the book All My Patients Are Under the Bed.

segments.title: Lila Miller and shelter medicine reform
segments.summary: Lila Miller, one of the first African American women to graduate from Cornell's Veterinary College, is called the mother of shelter medicine. Her reforms in the 1970s moved shelters away from mass killing toward adoption programs, vaccination and spaying and neutering, which sharply reduced euthanasia rates. The hosts discuss how pets moved indoors and how routine veterinary checkups became common, along with growing specialization and a shortage of large animal vets.

segments.title: Sponsor and local vet shout-out
segments.summary: Hosts give a personal shout-out to their local veterinary practice, Avondale Veterinary Hospital, with no paid sponsor read identified.

segments.title: Listener mail: Ian Bowers' tangents list
segments.summary: Hosts read a listener mail from Ian Bowers of Sandusky, Ohio, listing favorite past tangents and non sequiturs from earlier episodes, with brief comments on each.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and invite listeners to send their own listener mail.
